result.summary: Achilles drives the Trojans into the river Xanthus and slaughters them, killing Lycaon and Asteropaeus. The angry river attacks him, and Vulcan's fire at Juno's command subdues the river. The gods then fight each other, and Apollo draws Achilles away from the city by disguising himself as Agenor, while the Trojans flee inside the walls.

scenes.title: Slaughter in the river
scenes.summary: Achilles splits the Trojan host, kills many in the Xanthus, and takes twelve youths alive to sacrifice for Patroclus.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans face slaughter and being trapped; Achilles seeks vengeance for Patroclus.

scenes.title: Death of Lycaon
scenes.summary: Lycaon, once Achilles' captive, begs for mercy but is killed and thrown into the river.
scenes.stakes: Lycaon's life; he begs mercy and is refused.

scenes.title: Achilles kills Asteropaeus
scenes.summary: Xanthus emboldens the Paeonian Asteropaeus, who wounds Achilles slightly but is killed; Achilles boasts of descent from Jove.
scenes.stakes: Asteropaeus' life against Achilles; Achilles is slightly wounded.

scenes.title: The river attacks Achilles
scenes.summary: Xanthus protests, then floods Achilles and chases him. Neptune and Minerva reassure him, and Juno calls on Vulcan.
scenes.stakes: Achilles risks drowning ingloriously in the flood.

scenes.title: Vulcan's fire defeats Xanthus
scenes.summary: Vulcan burns the plain and river until Xanthus yields and swears to stop helping the Trojans.
scenes.stakes: Xanthus is being boiled and must yield.

scenes.title: The gods fight
scenes.summary: Minerva fells Mars and Venus, Juno beats Diana, and Apollo declines to fight Neptune. Diana complains to Jove, and the gods return to Olympus.
scenes.stakes: The gods' pride and standing; Diana is humiliated.

scenes.title: Agenor and Apollo's trick
scenes.summary: Priam orders the gates opened. Agenor stands against Achilles, and Apollo rescues him and lures Achilles away while the Trojans flee inside.
scenes.stakes: Troy may fall at once; Agenor risks death.

Apollo's image of mortals as leaves in summer.

analysis.text: Achilles' grief becomes pitiless rage: he refuses ransom, slaughters suppliants, and even fights a river, showing how war can overstep human limits.
The gods' comic battle contrasts with human suffering below, while Apollo and Jove keep fate on course for Troy's fall.

legacy.text: The Lycaon scene, with its supplication refused, is a model of pathos in epic and is often cited as a high point of Homer's battle narration.

fun_facts.text: Scamander is the real river of the Troad; Homer says gods call it Xanthus and men call it Scamander.

language_notes.text: Xanthus is the river's name among gods; mortals call it Scamander. It is called son of Jove because rivers were thought divine.
Achilles takes the twelve youths to be sacrificed on Patroclus' funeral pyre, a human sacrifice honoring the dead friend.
A guest-friend was a bound ally through hospitality, whose duties were sacred and often inherited; here he pays ransom for Lycaon.
Embracing the knees was the formal gesture of a suppliant begging for protection; it made killing him a religious offense.
The spear is said to be 'hungering for blood', treating the weapon as eager to kill.
'Idiot' is a blunt translation of a scornful address: Achilles calls Lycaon a fool for hoping for ransom.
'Vaunting' means boasting triumphantly over a defeated enemy.
"Within his waters" means in the river Xanthus's own stream; the river is a god and takes the slaughter as an offense.
"Pelian ash" refers to the spear of ash wood from Mount Pelion, which Achilles' father received as a gift.
"Foiled of its bloody banquet" pictures the spear as hungry for flesh; it missed the meal it was thrown to get.
"Fain" means eager or willing.
"Vaunting" means boasting; "spoiled him of his armour" means stripped him of it as plunder.
The Myrmidons are Achilles' followers from Phthia. Aeacus, Achilles' grandfather, was a son of Jove, which gives Achilles his divine descent.
Oceanus is the great world-encircling river believed to be the source of all waters. Achelous is a major Greek river, often treated as the greatest of rivers.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted or permitted; the river says Jove has allowed Achilles to destroy the Trojans.
Scamander is the river's name among men; Xanthus is the name the gods use. Both names refer to the same river.
"Straitly" means strictly or sternly; Jove gave a strict order.
The gardener's channel-clearing image is long; the dash interrupts it, and "even so" returns to the comparison with the river.
Achilles recalls Thetis's prophecy that he would die at Troy. Here he says she named Apollo's arrows as the cause.
Simois is the other river of Troy's plain, here called Scamander's brother.
"Forsooth" is an archaic word meaning "indeed"; here it is used sarcastically.
"Barrow" means burial mound. Denying him one would deny Achilles a proper funeral and lasting fame.
"Fain" means eager or willing; Juno says Xanthus is eager to fight Vulcan.
"The flood stayed" means the river's swollen waters were halted, since the fire dried up the plain.
Tamarisks are feathery-leaved shrubs or small trees that grow in damp, salty ground; the lotus here is a marsh plant, not the mythical fruit.
Faggots are bundles of dry sticks used as fuel.
Juno is Vulcan's mother and had urged him on against the river, so Xanthus appeals to her as the one who can restrain him.
Xanthus foretells the burning of Troy, an event after the Iliad's end, though the audience knew it well.
"These two" are Vulcan and the river Xanthus, whose fight ended when Juno made Vulcan stop burning the river.
"Set the gods by the ears" is an idiom meaning to make them quarrel.
Refers to the earlier battle when Minerva guided Diomed's spear into Mars, wounding him (Book 5).
A rood is an old unit of length, roughly six to eight yards, so the god's fall is enormous.
Mars's mother Juno is angry because he abandoned the Achaeans, whom she favours, after he had promised to help them.
Neptune recalls the gods' servitude to Laomedon, Priam's father, who cheated them of their wages when Troy's walls were built.
The "leaves in summer" image compares short-lived humans to leaves that fall; it echoes Homer's well-known leaves comparison.
"Far-Darter" is a standard epithet of Apollo, the archer god.
"Slayer of Argus" is an epithet of Mercury (Hermes), who killed the hundred-eyed Argus.
"Then had... taken" is an old conditional: the Achaeans would have taken the gates if Apollo had not intervened.
Ilius is Troy; Ida is the mountain range near Troy.
"Vouchsafes" means graciously grants; Jove gives Achilles his triumph as a favor.
"Fain" means willing or eager; Agenor is now ready to fight.
"The god's gift" is the divine armor made by Vulcan (Hephaestus) for Achilles, which turns the spear aside.
"Pell-mell" means in disorderly, headlong confusion.

context_notes.text: Tamarisk is a feathery shrub common along Mediterranean riverbanks; Achilles fights with sword alone, setting aside his spear.
Lemnos was an island in the northern Aegean, a place where captives were sold as slaves.
Denying burial and mourning was a terrible fate in Greek belief; the body should be laid out and lamented by family.
Trojans honored the river with sacrifices of bulls and living horses, so Achilles mocks their hope of its help.
Paeonia lay north of Greece, in the region of Macedonia. The Paeonians were Trojan allies. "Ilius" is Troy.
The shield with its layers of gold was made for Achilles by the god Hephaestus (Vulcan), which is why the gold is called a "gift of the god."
Saturn is the father of Jove (Greek Zeus). The river is a god, so it can take human form and speak.
Neptune (Greek Poseidon) is god of the sea and favours the Greeks. Pallas Minerva (Greek Athena) is also on their side.
Vulcan (Greek Hephaestus), Juno's lame son, is the god of fire and the forge. Hence he is called Crook-foot.
Xanthus is both the river and its god, also called Scamander. He rose in anger because Achilles was choking his stream with corpses.
Juno favours the Achaeans and hates Troy, yet she stops the fire because gods fighting over mortals goes too far.
The aegis is Minerva's tasselled goatskin shield, a fearsome divine weapon.
Neptune and Jove are brothers, so Neptune is Apollo's uncle, his father's brother.
Diana, goddess of the hunt, was said to kill women with her arrows, as Apollo killed men.
Leto is the mother of Apollo and Diana; Juno is jealous of her as one of Jove's lovers.
Antenor was a respected Trojan elder; his son Agenor is a capable warrior.
Apollo, a god who favored Troy, disguises himself as Agenor to draw Achilles away so the Trojans can reach safety.

literary_notes.text: Trojans fleeing into the river are compared to locusts driven into water by a grass fire, conveying panic and Achilles' fiery force.
Trojans are like fish fleeing a dolphin, casting Achilles as a predator who devours all he can catch.
Achilles' exaggerated fear that the slain might rise from the underworld shows his astonishment and growing rage.
Achilles, nearly invincible and godborn, admits his own coming death, using it to deny Lycaon pity and to level them as mortals.
Achilles' relentless vow of vengeance shows his grief for Patroclus has hardened into merciless wrath.
The graphic description of the wound and the darkness of death reflects the Iliad's unflinching, detailed treatment of battle deaths.
Achilles reasons that Jove outranks every river, so Jove's descendants outrank river-born men. He turns genealogy into a proof of his superiority.
A warrior who boasted of his river father is left to be eaten by river creatures, an ironic contrast with his claim of descent.
The river's roar is compared to a bull's bellowing, giving the flood a living, animal rage.
Achilles' flight is likened to a hunter-eagle's swoop, stressing his speed even while he runs in fear.
The peaceful gardener and his channel contrast with the deadly chase. The water outpaces its master, as the river outpaces Achilles.
The greatest warrior fears dying like a swineherd's boy swept away in a torrent, an inglorious death that mocks his heroic ideal.
Xanthus's scorn for Achilles' strength and armour reveals the river as proud, vengeful and personally insulted.
The drying of the plain is compared to a north wind drying an orchard, bringing the owner a homely, peaceful gladness amid war's horror.
The river is a speaking god who feels pain, scalded by flames, turning a natural event into a divine contest.
The boiling river is likened to a cauldron rendering hog fat, a domestic image that makes the river's suffering vivid and a little humiliating.
The river's mention of Troy burning anticipates the city's fall, which the poem never narrates directly.
The clash of gods is compared to a trumpet blare, conveying cosmic scale and noise.
Jove laughs with joy at the gods' brawl, treating their violence as entertainment, in contrast to mortal suffering.
The old boundary stone, a mark of order, becomes the weapon that fells the god of war.
Juno's humiliating beating of Diana with her own bow shows her formidable, domineering temper.
Diana's flight is likened to a dove escaping a falcon, emphasizing her helplessness against Juno.
Apollo's fear that the wall may fall before its time hints at Troy's destined doom.
Achilles' destruction is compared to the smoke of a city burned by angry gods, foreshadowing Troy's fate.
Achilles is shown as possessed, driven by a thirst for glory beyond ordinary limits.
Agenor's inner debate reveals his fear and his sense of honor, humanizing a minor warrior.
Agenor is likened to a leopardess who fights on despite wounds, stressing his stubborn courage born of desperation.
Achilles believes he is about to catch his prey, yet he is chasing a god who is deliberately deceiving him.
